title: Profile Shapes & Day Types

lessons.title: Recognising profile shapes
lessons.desc: Go through the last twenty session profiles on ES and label each D, P, b, thin or double. Keep the list next to your IB log.

lessons.title: P and b days
lessons.desc: For every P or b day in your list, write what happened next session at the heavy node near the extreme: accepted, rejected or ignored. This is your own evidence on how much the traditional reading is worth on your instrument.

bodyHtml:
Once you can build a profile, the next skill is recognising what kind of day produced it. Profiles come in a handful of recurring shapes, and Market Profile practitioners group whole sessions into day types based on the size of the initial balance and how far the day extended beyond it. Knowing the shape and the day type won't tell you what happens tomorrow. It tells you what kind of auction just happened, which is the context for everything you do next.

This chapter uses both the volume profile from VP-03 and the TPO letters from VP-02. The readings attached to each shape ("short covering", "long liquidation" and so on) are common interpretations in the profile literature, not facts about who traded.

The D shape: a balanced auction

A D-shaped profile is fattest in the middle and thins out toward the high and the low, like the bell curve that originally inspired Market Profile. Most of the day's trade happened in the centre, and both extremes saw little business. It is the picture of a balanced day in auction terms: buyers and sellers broadly agreed on value, and probes of the edges were rejected.

Practitioners treat a D-shaped day as a signal that the market is waiting for new information. The next day's open relative to this value area (inside it or outside it) becomes the first clue about whether the balance continues.

The P and b shapes

A P-shaped profile has its bulk near the top and a long, thin stem below. Price started low, moved up quickly through the lower prices (leaving little volume there) and then spent the rest of the session trading near the high. A b-shaped profile is the mirror image: a quick move down through thin prices, then a heavy node near the low.

The traditional reading of a P is short covering: sellers who were short buy back to close, which pushes price up quickly, and once they are done the market settles into balance near the high. The traditional reading of a b is long liquidation: holders of long positions sell out, price drops, and it settles near the low. The reason these readings matter is that covering and liquidation are one-off flows. Once they are finished, the push can fade. Treat them as hypotheses to test against the following session, not as conclusions.

Thin profiles and double distributions

A thin, elongated profile has volume spread evenly across a wide range with no clear bulge. Price never stayed anywhere long enough to build a node. That is the profile of a trend: the market kept moving to find the other side.

A double distribution has two separate nodes with a thin valley between them. The market balanced in one area, moved quickly to another, and balanced again. You saw the same pattern in VP-01 as "balance, imbalance, new balance". The low-volume valley between the two nodes is a price area traders mark, because the market passed through it without doing business there.

Day types from the initial balance

Day types classify the whole session by two things: how wide the initial balance (IB) was, and how far price extended beyond it. The standard set from the Market Profile literature is below. Each figure is an illustrative TPO profile built from period data; the gold bar on the left marks the IB.

Normal day. A wide IB contains the whole session. The opening hour found both sides quickly, and nobody pushed price outside it later.

Normal variation day. A moderate IB with range extension on one side, usually by a similar distance to the IB itself. In plain terms: an opening range and one push out of it.

Trend day. A narrow IB followed by persistent extension in one direction, each period trading mostly above (or below) the one before. The profile is thin and the close tends to be near the extreme. These are the days when fading every move back to value is most dangerous.

Neutral day. Range extension on both sides of the IB. Practitioners split it into a neutral centre day, which closes back in the middle of the range, and a neutral extreme day, which closes near one end, read as one side winning late in the session.

Non-trend day. A very narrow IB and a very narrow day, with little extension. Nobody was willing to push price anywhere. These often come before scheduled news or on holiday-thin sessions.

A double-distribution trend day is a common variation: the day balances in one area, breaks out, and builds a second balance, giving the double-distribution shape from earlier on a single session.

Worked example: classifying a session step by step

Use the trend-day profile above as the session to classify.

  1. Measure the IB. Periods A and B traded from 5,198 to 5,202, so the IB is 4 points. Compare that with the last ten days in your IB log from VP-02. For this example, assume it is narrower than usual.
  2. Check for range extension. Period C traded above the IB high. There was no extension below.
  3. Check persistence. Each later period traded mostly above the previous one, and the final period printed the day's high at 5,217.
  4. Look at the shape. No row has more than two letters. It is thin and elongated, with no dominant node.
  5. Classify. Narrow IB, one-sided extension of 15 points, persistent period-by-period progress, thin profile: a trend day up.
  6. Record the implications for tomorrow. Mark the day's high and the single prints left in the middle of the range. Tomorrow's first question is whether the market accepts prices above the high or comes back into the thin area.

Day types are easiest to classify at the close, but profile traders form a working guess during the session. After the IB forms, you already know whether it is narrow or wide. The first range extension, and whether it holds, narrows the possibilities further. Treat the guess as provisional and update it as letters build. Timing matters too: the extensions that define a day often come during the killzones covered in the core course (chapter 13).

Using yesterday's shape today

The shape and day type are most useful as context for the next session. A few pairings come up often in the profile literature. Treat each as a question to ask, not an answer.

D shape / normal day

Question for today: Does balance continue, or does the market break out?

What would answer it: Open inside value and rotate = balance; open outside and hold there = breakout

P shape

Question for today: Was the rally short covering that has now finished?

What would answer it: Price fails to build new value above the heavy node, or trades back into the thin stem

b shape

Question for today: Was the sell-off long liquidation that has now finished?

What would answer it: Price fails to build new value below the heavy node, or trades back into the thin area above

Trend day

Question for today: Does the trend continue, or does the market balance?

What would answer it: Acceptance beyond yesterday's extreme, or a return into yesterday's single prints

Double distribution

Question for today: Which of the two nodes is value now?

What would answer it: Where the market spends time and builds volume after the open

Notice that every answer is something you observe after the open: acceptance or rejection, time spent, volume built. That is the auction-theory habit from VP-01 applied to a new session. The profile gives you the question; the next session's trading gives you the answer.

Common mistakes

  • Deciding the day type too early. A day that looks like a trend day at 11:00 can become a neutral day by the close.
  • Reading P and b as certain facts about who traded. "Short covering" is an interpretation of the shape, not information about positions.
  • Ignoring context. A D-shaped day in the middle of a larger uptrend means something different from a D-shaped day at a multi-day high. Check the higher timeframe (chapter 04).
  • Forcing every day into a box. Some sessions don't fit neatly. Record them as "unclear" rather than bending the definition.
  • Fading trend days. The standard error on a trend day is to keep selling "expensive" prices. On a trend day, the market is still searching for the other side.

Key takeaways

  • D = balanced; P and b = one-sided move then balance near the extreme; thin = trend; double distribution = two balances.
  • Day types are defined by IB width and range extension: normal, normal variation, trend, neutral (centre or extreme), non-trend.
  • The readings attached to shapes are interpretations. Test them against what happens next.
  • Classify during the day provisionally, then confirm at the close.

Practice exercises

  1. Label the shape (D, P, b, thin, double) of each of the last twenty ES session profiles.
  2. Using your IB log from VP-02, classify the same twenty sessions by day type. Note any that don't fit.
  3. For every P and b day, write down what the next session did relative to the node near the extreme.
  4. During one live session, write your provisional day type at 10:30, 12:00 and 14:00 New York time, then compare with the final result.

Self-check quiz

1. What does a D-shaped profile suggest about the auction?

Balance: most trade happened in the middle, and both extremes were rejected quickly.

2. What is the traditional reading of a P-shaped profile?

Short covering: a quick move up through thin prices followed by balance near the high. It is an interpretation, not a fact about positions.

3. How does a normal day differ from a normal variation day?

On a normal day the wide IB contains the whole session. On a normal variation day price extends beyond the IB on one side.

4. What makes a day "neutral"?

Range extension on both sides of the IB. Where it closes decides neutral centre or neutral extreme.

5. Why is fading moves particularly risky on a trend day?

Because the market keeps moving to find the other side, and prices that look expensive relative to earlier value keep getting accepted.

  3. Time price opportunity charts explained - TradingView Help Center
  4. Volume profile indicators: basic concepts - TradingView Help Center
  5. Mind Over Markets, Updated Edition (Dalton, Jones, Dalton; Wiley 2013) - further reading on day types
